title: Build your own provider - the mock, and what it is not

questions.prompt: The MockProvider's FORMAT_SHIFT dict shifts the noul probability by -0.81 when the state is nested instead of prose. Why does the mock simulate that at all?
options: Because the mock is a faithful copy of TypeSafe Jev and reproduces its real behaviour
Because the mock reproduces the SHAPE of published findings so the friction pipeline has something to detect, with zero credentials and zero spend
Because the mock was trained on the routing battery and learned the shift
Because the mock needs some way to make its own output look interesting
questions.explain: The mock's own docstring says it reproduces the *shape* of the published findings so the pipeline - metrics, swap matrix, format-friction report - can be exercised without API keys. The shift is a hard-coded simulation of the reported format-friction effect, so `python -m decisionarena friction --provider mock` has a real signal to find. The first option is wrong: the mock is not a copy of any model and knows nothing about Jev. The third option is wrong: there is no training here at all - FORMAT_SHIFT is a literal dict of three constants. The fourth option is wrong: the shift exists so the harness is exercised, not to look impressive; report.run_report() stamps mock runs with a SIMULATED RUN banner precisely because the numbers are not evidence.

questions.prompt: Why must a mock provider be deterministic rather than random, even though the mock's numbers are not published as evidence?
options: Because a random mock would be too slow to run over a whole battery
Because a random mock would consume API credits
Because randomness makes the numbers look more realistic
Because a random mock makes it impossible to tell whether a change in your metrics code caused a change in the score
questions.explain: Determinism is what makes the harness testable. If the mock rolled differently on every call, a change in your metric code and a change in the mock's output would be indistinguishable, and you could never write a regression test for the metrics. That is why the mock derives every number from a hash of seed + question id + serialised state - a pure function of its inputs - so repeats are stable. The speed option is wrong: hashing is cheap. The credits option is wrong: the mock never touches the network, so there is nothing to bill. The realism option is wrong and dangerously backwards - the mock's job is to be reproducible and clearly labelled, not to look real.

questions.prompt: What does changing the seed of MockProvider(seed="other-seed") actually change, and what does it let you do?
options: It changes how many tokens the mock reports, so the cost accounting changes
It makes the mock talk to a different vendor
It changes every number the mock derives from its hash, reproducibly - so two different seeds behave like two different models you can compare offline
It changes only the format-friction shift
questions.explain: The seed is the first component of the hashed string, so changing it changes the hash, which changes the uniform number the mock derives and therefore every probability it produces - and it does so reproducibly. Two mocks with different seeds therefore behave like two different 'models', which is exactly how you exercise label_agreement, probability_gap and action_change_rate without spending money. The token option is wrong: the token estimate is computed from the length of the state and the questions, not from the seed. The vendor option is wrong: the mock never makes a network call. The format option is wrong: FORMAT_SHIFT is a class attribute, identical for every mock instance.

questions.prompt: You run the whole battery with --provider mock and get accuracy 80 %. What can you honestly conclude from that number?
options: That the runner, the metrics and the report all work end to end on a stable, reproducible input - and nothing whatsoever about a real model
That the mock model is 80 % accurate at routing tickets
That a real provider would score at least as well, because the battery is the same
That the spend cap worked, so the run is a valid measurement
questions.explain: The mock proves the machinery: the battery loads, the provider is called, answers are normalised, the metrics compute, the report renders, and the raw JSONL evidence is written. The number itself is a property of MockProvider's hash, not of any model. The second option is the exact mistake the repo's rule 4 forbids - report.run_report() even prints a SIMULATED RUN banner saying the numbers must never be quoted as evidence. The third option is wrong because the mock's accuracy is arbitrary; the battery being identical does not make the mock a proxy for a provider. The fourth option confuses cost control with validity: a successful spend-cap check says nothing about whether a number is meaningful.
